extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of political philosophy, history, and public affairs
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and argumentative standards for assessing revolutions, political societies, and reform measures, emphasizing prudence, institutional continuity, social prerequisites of liberty, and the proper public conduct of clubs and clergy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty must be combined with government and social institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberty is not a benefit unless it is combined with government, public force, disciplined armies, an effective and well-distributed revenue, morality and religion, solidity of property, peace and order, and civil and social manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke: 'I should... suspend my congratulations on the new liberty of France until I was informed how it had been combined with government, with public force, with the discipline and obedience of armies, with the collection of an effective and well-distributed revenue, with morality and religion, with the solidity of property, with peace and order, with civil and social manners.' Anti-pattern: praising abstract liberty without checking institutions and social conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspend judgment until initial effervescence subsides
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not prematurely congratulate or endorse a new revolution; wait until the first effervescence is subsided and the real use of power becomes evident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke insists prudence: 'we ought to suspend our judgement until the first effervescence is a little subsided, till the liquor is cleared,' because early enthusiasm can conceal long-term effects. Scoring note: favors caution and empirical observation over immediate praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context and circumstances determine the effect of abstract principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract political principles (like 'liberty') acquire their moral and practical character only in particular circumstances; one cannot evaluate actions on purely metaphysical abstractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke: 'Circumstances... give in reality to every political principle its distinguishing color and discriminating effect.' Anti-pattern: applying abstract formulas without considering local institutions, customs, and social fabric.

rubrics_metrics.name: The pulpit should avoid partisan political agitprop
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious pulpits should not be used as platforms for intense political agitation; church speech ought to be the 'healing voice of Christian charity' not political harangue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke criticizes Dr. Price's sermon as mixing politics and religion and reviving a dangerous pulpit style. Example of anti-pattern: sermons that incite and politicize congregations, spreading unmoderated doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public political declarations need transparency and signatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Addresses or resolutions claiming public or national authority should be accompanied by the names of signatories so the world can judge their number, character, and authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke objects to the Revolution Society's anonymous collective resolution: 'Their signatures ought, in my opinion, to have been annexed to their instrument.' Guidance: anonymous authority is a political stratagem that falsely inflates importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority-only resolutions are weaker than reasoned argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Votes and resolutions that rest 'solely on authority' are less convincing than arguments; public political acts should rely on reason, not merely authority of a small group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke: 'If what this society has thought proper to send forth had been a piece of argument, it would have signified little whose argument it was. But this is only a vote and resolution. It stands solely on authority.' Anti-pattern: appealing to prestige or clubs instead of substantive argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not derive general legal principles from special, exceptional cases
rubrics_metrics.description: It is improper to take a law or event enacted for a particular circumstance and treat it as a universal principle; 'privilegium non transit in exemplum.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke argues the temporary settlement under King William should not be used to claim a general elective right to the crown. Scoring: emphasizes respect for precedent and legal continuity over extrapolation from exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal continuity and settled succession as foundations of stability
rubrics_metrics.description: The Declaration of Right and settled hereditary succession embody foundational constitutional principles; abrupt claims to a popular right to choose governors undermine unity, peace, and tranquillity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke contrasts the sober, lawyer-drawn Declaration of Right with revolutionary claims: 'Not one word is said, nor one suggestion made, of a general right

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware revolutionary doctrines preserved as future instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract doctrines (e.g., that the people have a right to choose governors) may be taught now as harmless theory but kept 'in reserve' to be used later — a dangerous political strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke warns that propagators 'hope that their abstract principle ... would be overlooked' and 'laid by for future use.' Anti-pattern: promoting radical principles under the guise of harmless theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political clubs/societies should not usurp diplomatic or national representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Private societies must not presume a public diplomatic capacity or be treated by foreign assemblies as 'privileged persons' without legitimate authorization from the nation they claim to represent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke: Revolution Society became a kind of 'privileged persons' and 'a kind of committee in England for extending the principles of the National Assembly.' Guidance: bodies acting as quasi-diplomatic agents without mandate risk deception and instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative schemes must preserve a connection between constituent and legislator
rubrics_metrics.description: Electoral or constitutional designs in which the first constituent voter has no connection with the representative legislator are fundamentally vicious and absurd.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke criticizes French proposals where 'the first constituent voter has no connection with the representative legislator.' Scoring: values accountable, connected representation over abstractly constructed bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid wholesale destruction and the ideology of 'everything must be destroyed'
rubrics_metrics.description: Schemes that resolve to 'change everything... all to be destroyed' are reckless; salutary reform should not start from a presumption of universal demolition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke quotes an assemblyman who advocates remaking everything: 'tout detruire; oui, tout detruire; puis que tout est a recreer' and treats this as an alarming, irresponsible doctrine. Anti-pattern: ideological maxim that legitimizes plunder and social ruin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess who truly wields power, not merely those most visible
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating a political movement, observe the actual use of power and who the real movers are, since the most stirring figures may not be the real directors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke: 'considerate people... will observe the use which is made of power and particularly of so trying a thing as new power in new persons.' Guidance: distinguish rhetoricians from operators; evaluate institutional control and practical outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence: prefer anxious apprehension to complacent security
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better to be 'despised for too anxious apprehensions than ruined by too confident a security.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke uses this maxim to justify cautious foreign and domestic policy responses to neighboring upheavals. Scoring: favors precautionary principle in statecraft.
